Grid resolution and computational cost

Source: vignettes/grid-resolution.Rmd
grid-resolution.Rmd

Does a finer grid give a better accessibility index, and what does it cost? A raster gives every place explicit geometry and lines all inputs up cell by cell. Its cost grows with the number of cells times the number of facilities, while the result can be no better than the demand and travel data behind it. This guide runs the enhanced two-step floating catchment area (E2SFCA) index of Getting started, which gives each place the GP supply per resident within reach, with weights that fall with travel time. It runs the index at the native resolution of the bundled grids, at two coarser resolutions and at one finer resolution, and compares results, size and run time. By the end you can estimate the memory a grid needs and check whether a coarser grid would change your answer. The inputs are the mainland grids of The Cornwall GP example data. The spax() interface and the allocation model are experimental and may change in later versions.

library(spax)
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)

The inputs

The setup code shared by every grid guide, explained in The Cornwall GP example data, reads the population grid (residents per cell), the mainland practices with their GP full-time equivalents (FTE), and one layer of travel minutes per practice.

gp <- cornwall_gp |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
pop <- read_spax_example("cornwall_pop.tif")
travel_grid <- read_spax_example("cornwall_gp_travel.tif")[[gp$practice]]
# Keep cells with a travel time to every mainland practice
pop <- trim(mask(pop, sum(travel_grid)))
travel_grid <- crop(travel_grid, pop)
grid_data <- prep_data(pop, gp, travel_grid, id_col = "practice", supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg")

grid_data is the native-resolution input. Below, index_at() prepares each resolution the same way.

What one cell-by-practice array costs

The travel grid holds one value per cell and practice, and the decay weights hold another array of the same size. The numeric payload of one such array is cells times practices times 8 bytes.

cells <- c(grid = ncell(pop), populated = sum(!is.na(values(pop))))

# 8 bytes per value, one value per cell and practice
data.frame(
  cells,
  practices = nrow(gp),
  MiB_per_array = round(cells * nrow(gp) * 8 / 1024^2, 1)
)
          cells practices MiB_per_array
grid      21879        54           9.0
populated  6912        54           2.8

The rectangular grid has 3.2 times as many cells as its populated part, because it also covers sea and land outside Cornwall. That is small here. The same arithmetic at 100 meters, or with hundreds of facilities, reaches gigabytes. spax reads the rasters in blocks of rows when it computes an FCA index, so it needs less memory than holding these arrays whole. Measure memory and run time on the whole workflow: object.size() of a terra raster reports only a pointer, not the cell values.

Change the resolution

Demand counts can be added up exactly when cells are merged. Travel cannot: the bundled grids do not contain the road network, so a coarse cell’s travel time has to be approximated from its fine cells. Here we use the resident-weighted mean of the fine-cell minutes. Averaging travel before a nonlinear decay does not give averaged weights, so this is one explicit approximation. For a real study, recompute travel at the target resolution if you can.

A factor of 2 merges each 2 x 2 block of cells into one, 4 merges 4 x 4 blocks, and 0.5 splits each cell into four. The four subcells of a split cell each get a quarter of its residents and keep its travel times. This adds cells but no information.

# Demand and travel grids at `factor` times the native cell width
at_resolution <- function(factor) {
  # Native grid: unchanged
  if (factor == 1) return(list(demand = pop, travel = travel_grid))

  # Finer grid: split residents evenly, copy the parent's travel times
  if (factor < 1) {
    split <- round(1 / factor)
    return(list(
      demand = disagg(pop, split) / split^2,
      travel = disagg(travel_grid, split)
    ))
  }

  # Coarser grid: add up residents, take resident-weighted mean minutes
  demand <- aggregate(pop, factor, fun = "sum", na.rm = TRUE)
  minutes <- aggregate(travel_grid * pop, factor, fun = "sum", na.rm = TRUE) /
    demand
  list(demand = demand, travel = minutes)
}

factors <- c(0.5, 1, 2, 4)
grids <- lapply(factors, at_resolution)

Now time the E2SFCA at each resolution, with the Gaussian decay of the other guides: a travel scale σ of 10 minutes, at which a practice 10 minutes away keeps 61% of its weight. The timings are elapsed seconds on the machine that built this guide, the median of three runs. Read them as relative costs.

e2sfca_spec <- spec_e2sfca(decay = decay_gaussian(sigma = 10))

# The E2SFCA index on one resolution's grids
index_at <- function(grid) {
  resolution_data <- prep_data(
    grid$demand,
    gp,
    grid$travel,
    id_col = "practice",
    supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg"
  )
  spax(resolution_data, e2sfca_spec)
}

# Median elapsed seconds of three runs at each resolution
seconds <- sapply(grids, function(grid) {
  median(replicate(3, system.time(index_at(grid))[["elapsed"]]))
})

results <- lapply(grids, index_at)

To compare the results, take each surface back to the native grid: every native cell gets the value of the cell that contains it. Then compare cell by cell, weighting by native residents.

# The native surface and residents, one value per native cell
native <- 1000 * values(results[[2]]$accessibility, mat = FALSE)
residents <- values(pop, mat = FALSE)

# One table row per resolution
summary_row <- function(level) {
  # This surface on the native grid
  on_native <- resample(results[[level]]$accessibility, pop, method = "near")
  on_native <- 1000 * values(on_native, mat = FALSE)

  # Residents and cell area on this resolution's own grid
  demand <- values(grids[[level]]$demand, mat = FALSE)
  area <- values(cellSize(grids[[level]]$demand, unit = "km"), mat = FALSE)

  # Index per 1,000 on its own grid, and the change from the native surface
  own <- 1000 * values(results[[level]]$accessibility, mat = FALSE)
  change <- abs(on_native / native - 1)

  data.frame(
    factor = factors[level],
    cell_km2 = round(mean(area[!is.na(demand)]), 2),
    cells = sum(!is.na(demand)),
    seconds = seconds[level],
    mean_per_1000 = round(weighted.mean(own, demand, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    median_change_pct = round(
      100 * median(change[!is.na(residents)], na.rm = TRUE),
      1
    ),
    mean_change_pct = round(
      100 * weighted.mean(change, residents, na.rm = TRUE),
      1
    )
  )
}

comparison <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_along(factors), summary_row))
comparison
  factor cell_km2 cells seconds mean_per_1000 median_change_pct mean_change_pct
1    0.5     0.14 27648   0.528         0.575               0.0             0.0
2    1.0     0.55  6912   0.069         0.575               0.0             0.0
3    2.0     2.20  1829   0.015         0.575               1.8             1.4
4    4.0     8.79   506   0.011         0.575               3.3             2.5

cells counts the populated cells, and cell_km2 is their mean area in square kilometers. The native cells are 30 arc-seconds, often called 1 km: about 0.93 km north to south but only about 0.59 km east to west at this latitude. The two change columns give the median and the resident-weighted mean of the absolute percentage change from the native surface, over native cells.

Some things stay fixed. Every resolution keeps the same 541,184 residents, and the resident-weighted mean index (mean_per_1000) stays at total GP FTE per 1,000 residents, because both FCA steps use the same weights. That identity says nothing about local accuracy.

What changes:

  • Finer cells (factor 0.5) give 4 times as many populated cells and take 7.7 times as long, yet reproduce the native surface exactly (a change of 0%): no information was added.
  • Coarser cells are cheaper: the 4 x 4 grid runs 6.3 times as fast as the native one, though on a grid this small every run takes a fraction of a second. The local pattern changes by 1.4% to 2.5% for the average resident. A 10-minute decay is wide compared with cells of 2.2 to 8.8 square kilometers, which likely keeps the change small. Repeat the comparison for a shorter travel scale or a binary catchment.

The maps put the native surface and the 4 x 4 surface on one color scale.

# The native surface and the 4 x 4 surface, both on the native grid
pair <- c(
  1000 * results[[2]]$accessibility,
  resample(1000 * results[[4]]$accessibility, pop, method = "near")
)
names(pair) <- c("Native grid", "Aggregated 4 x 4")
# Mainland Cornwall's outline, in the grid's longitude and latitude
outline <- cornwall_lsoa |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_union() |>
  vect()

plot(
  pair,
  axes = FALSE,
  col = hcl.colors(50, "viridis"),
  range = range(values(pair), na.rm = TRUE),
  mar = c(1, 1, 2, 6),
  plg = list(title = "GP FTE\nper 1,000"),
  fun = function() lines(outline, lwd = 0.5)
)

The coarse surface keeps the broad pattern but blurs the local detail, including the low values on Bodmin Moor, the upland north-east of the map’s center. Its blocks also cover cells that the native grid leaves empty at the coast.

The allocation model

The allocation model of Where do residents register? estimates the share of each place’s residents who register with each practice. On the small areas, its travel matrix of areas by practices is small. On raster data every populated cell becomes an origin, a place residents start from, so the matrix is the cell-by-practice array above. In the large example of ?prep_data, a fit to practice totals from one start peaks at about 8 times that matrix, and the help page gives its run time too. Read only the tables you need: as.data.frame(result, type = "facilities") (one row per practice) or type = "origins" (one row per origin) is far smaller than type = "flows", which has a row for every origin and practice with a positive flow. The bootstrap of How sure are the estimates? refits the model for every draw, so its run time grows with the number of draws.
